<reason>Side A built the stronger path to victory by consistently pressing the geometric constraint of finite urban land against permanent burial allocations. A exposed fatal contradictions in Side B's alternatives—lease systems violate religious covenants against exhumation, while mausoleums abandon the in-ground burial B claimed was non-negotiable. A's pressure questions forced B to confront the inevitable filling of "dedicated sections," and B's retreat to "future expansion" and peri-urban coordination conceded that permanent urban burial is temporary, validating A's transition argument. While B mounted a powerful defense of religious liberty and cultural dignity, it failed to refute the core land-scarcity logic or answer what happens when the cemetery is full, leaving A with the decisive comparative advantage on the proposition as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 (A4.1-A4.6), which directly answered both pressure questions and exposed that Side B's plan inevitably ends with peri-urban religious cemeteries—the very solution B had criticized as an unjust travel burden—while demonstrating that circular memorials (columbaria, memorial groves) preserve permanent visitation without monopolizing scarce land, thus keeping public cemeteries open indefinitely.</best_rebuttal>
